r: The course builds entry-level HR literacy spanning employment law, HR information systems, sourcing, recruiting, onboarding, workplace safety, and separation procedures. Several applied tasks it targets — screening candidates, drafting job postings, populating HRIS records, and generating onboarding paperwork — sit inside administrative and information-processing work that observed-usage data already shows AI performing competently, and applicant-tracking systems have automated resume screening for years. Employment-law compliance and termination decisions carry real liability exposure, sustaining near-term human oversight, and the course's soft-skills and interpersonal-relations component resists full automation. At 24 months, diffusion into small and mid-size employer HR functions remains uneven, and the course still functions as prerequisite grounding for further HR coursework. The rating is Medium: routine HR administration is already meaningfully automatable, but adoption lag and the interpersonal residue keep the instrumental need for the course from collapsing this early.

By 2031, AI HR platforms will plausibly handle most sourcing, screening, HRIS reporting, and onboarding documentation with limited human drafting, and observed-usage growth in business-and-office tasks supports that trajectory. Task-exposure research classifies this kind of administrative information work as comparatively exposed. The interpersonal residue — employee relations, workplace-safety judgment, termination conversations — remains real but is a narrower share of the course's content than the administrative core, and the foundational role this course plays for later HR coursework caps rather than eliminates the erosion. The rating rises to High: the bulk of the applied HR-administration tasks the course teaches are broadly automatable by this horizon, even though a human HR professional still exercises judgment on the highest-stakes, most interpersonal matters the course also covers.

A decade out, AI is plausibly embedded across the HR technology stack — sourcing, screening, onboarding, records management, and much compliance drafting — with human HR professionals concentrated on employee-relations judgment, termination decisions, and oversight of automated systems. The instrumental case for a course teaching HR administration as a set of tasks to perform personally is substantially eroded; the residual need shifts toward supervising and verifying AI-mediated HR workflows. The rating holds High, hedged by genuine uncertainty about how much interpersonal HR work — conflict resolution, culture-building, sensitive terminations — resists automation even under aggressive capability growth. Capability-trend evidence on how quickly AI task-time horizons are lengthening supports treating this shift as advanced well before 2036 rather than as a distant possibility. The foundational role for downstream HR coursework persists but does not by itself pull the rating back to Medium at this horizon.
MGT 1260.d: This course introduces students to the acumen that is requisite for entry into a career in Human Resources (HR). Participants in this course explore business fundamentals, functions and trends and their relationship to HR; and what a contemporary HR practice entails. Focus is placed on the acquisition of a foundational level of knowledge in the areas of employment law, human resource information systems, sourcing, recruiting and assessing candidates, onboarding and retaining employees, workplace safety, employer and employee rights; and what an HR professional needs to attend to when it comes to employee separation/ termination. Students further develop the soft skills, problem solving and performance that are requisite to fulfill the role of an entry-level HR professional. This course also features an exploration of the various career paths that are available to those who choose a career in HR.

r: The course places students in an approved employer setting to perform actual professional work, explore career paths, and build workplace professionalism — an experiential placement rather than a body of transferable instructional content. Whatever administrative subtasks a given internship involves may be individually exposed to AI, but the instrumental purpose of the course is the student's own embodied participation in a real workplace: reporting to supervisors, functioning within a team, and being professionally evaluated in person. Task-exposure research's low-exposure categories map naturally onto this kind of situated, interpersonal, in-person work experience. There is no substitute an AI system performs on the student's behalf, since the credit is earned by presence and performance in the placement itself. At 24 months the instrumental need is intact and essentially untouched by AI capability growth.

By 2031, AI tools will likely handle more of the discrete administrative tasks a given internship placement might assign a student, and employers will increasingly expect interns to work alongside AI systems rather than perform manual busywork. But the course's instrumental function — a student physically present in a workplace, supervised, evaluated, and building professional relationships in real time — is not something AI performs for the student; embodiment and real-time interpersonal presence keep the requirement in place. Diffusion of AI into employer workflows generally is still uneven across firm size and sector at this horizon. The rating remains Low: the specific tasks an intern is assigned may shift toward AI-adjacent work, but the need for the student to be there, doing it, does not erode.

A decade out, workplaces will likely be substantially reorganized around AI-assisted work, and the content of what any given internship exposes a student to will look different from today. Even so, the course's binding rationale is experiential and embodied — a student personally gaining supervised professional experience, feedback, and workplace socialization — which is categorically distinct from a task an AI system executes on the learner's behalf. Wide uncertainty applies to what internships will look like inside AI-saturated workplaces, but not to whether direct workplace experience remains instrumentally necessary for career entry. Diffusion research on uneven firm-level AI adoption suggests workplace transformation will be gradual and inconsistent across the small and mid-size employers that typically host business internships, reinforcing rather than undermining the embodied rationale. The rating holds Low; confidence is limited chiefly because the brief catalog description gives little task-level detail to anchor the horizon-specific claims.
MGT 1985.d: Approved internships introduce the specific field of business as well as provide an opportunity to gain practical, hands-on professional work experience. Students will learn about the profession, explore related career paths, and increase professionalism.

r: The course teaches students to analyze statutes, cases, and regulatory materials covering agency, contracts, torts, and business organizations. This kind of doctrinal legal analysis and case summarization is a task category where general-purpose language models already perform competently, and observed-usage data shows document analysis and drafting as a substantial share of current AI use. The course is explicit prerequisite substrate — Legal Environment II, International Business Law, and Employment and HR Law within this same department all require it — which anchors the rating below what raw task-exposure alone would suggest. At 24 months the instrumental need to build this foundational legal-reasoning vocabulary is only modestly eroded: AI can summarize case holdings, but the course's downstream role in the curriculum is untouched by that capability.

By 2031, AI legal-research tools will fluently brief cases, explain statutory frameworks, and analyze contract and tort scenarios of the kind this course covers, and jagged-frontier evidence on AI legal-citation errors argues for continued human verification rather than for eliminating the underlying literacy. Task-exposure research places this analytical, document-centered work among more exposed categories. Because the course is prerequisite scaffolding for three later required courses in this same sequence, its instrumental role is capped rather than removed by that exposure, but the rating still rises to High as the direct analytical tasks — reading and summarizing legal materials — become broadly AI-performed with limited need for a student to do so unassisted. Observed-usage data reinforces this trajectory, showing document analysis and drafting already a substantial and growing share of professional AI use.

A decade out, AI legal-analysis tools are plausibly a routine part of business legal work, competently drafting summaries and issue-spotting memos of the kind introductory business-law coursework once trained students to produce by hand. The instrumental case for personally performing this analytical work is substantially eroded, with residual value concentrated in verifying AI-generated legal analysis for citation accuracy and jurisdictional fit — a real but narrower need than the course's full content. Capability-trend evidence on lengthening AI task-time horizons makes this shift plausible well within the decade, even accounting for the deliberate pace at which legal-education curricula typically change. The rating holds High, hedged by genuine uncertainty over how much legal-education pedagogy shifts toward AI-output verification rather than original analysis, and by the course's continuing structural role as prerequisite substrate for the three downstream courses that still require it in the catalog.
MGT 2210.d: This course is designed to present the legal system as it applies to business. The course includes a discussion of fundamental concepts related to the nature and sources of law and to the resolution of disputes. The course requires analysis of statutes, cases, and regulations of related governmental agencies that address employment, securities, trade and workplace decisions. The law of agency, contracts, organizations and torts is analyzed. Ethical and international aspects of law are treated where appropriate.

r: The course teaches entrepreneurial-mindset development and techniques for enhancing creativity and innovative thinking, applied to identifying unmet needs and market opportunities. Generative AI tools already assist substantially with ideation, brainstorming, and opportunity-scanning tasks, and observed-usage data shows writing and idea-generation support as a prominent current use case. The course's purpose, though, is cultivating the student's own creative and opportunity-recognition capacity, not merely producing venture-idea documents, and it functions as prerequisite grounding for the feasibility-analysis coursework that follows it. At 24 months the instrumental need is only partially eroded: AI can generate candidate venture ideas quickly, but Diffusion of these generative tools into standard entrepreneurship-education practice is still uneven this early, and productivity research on AI-assisted writing shows the largest gains accruing to less-experienced users rather than wholesale task replacement, so the course's technique-building purpose and its role preparing students for subsequent entrepreneurship coursework keep the near-term rating at Medium rather than lower.

By 2031, AI ideation and market-opportunity-scanning tools will plausibly generate venture concepts, competitive scans, and creativity-technique exercises with much of the fluency this course currently develops through practice. Task-exposure research places brainstorming and written ideation among more automatable activities, and no institutional mandate or embodiment protects the course. The instrumental case shifts toward evaluating and refining AI-generated venture concepts rather than generating them from scratch, and the course's single-course scaffolding role for feasibility analysis is a modest, not decisive, constraint. Productivity research on AI-assisted writing and idea generation shows substantial time savings alongside quality gains, a pattern consistent with treating opportunity-scanning and concept documentation as largely automatable by this horizon. The rating rises to High: the applied creativity-and-opportunity-identification tasks the course targets are largely performable by AI, even though a human founder's judgment about which opportunities to pursue retains real value.

A decade out, AI systems will plausibly generate and evaluate venture concepts at a scale and speed no individual course exercise replicates, and the central case has such tools embedded throughout early-stage entrepreneurship work. The instrumental need to personally practice ideation and opportunity-identification techniques is substantially eroded; what likely remains is the founder's judgment in selecting, committing to, and pursuing a specific opportunity under real resource constraints — a narrower residual than the full course content. Capability-trend research on lengthening AI task-time horizons supports extrapolating today's ideation gains into fuller opportunity-identification competence by 2036, even as genuine uncertainty remains about entrepreneurial judgment specifically. The rating holds High, with a genuine hedge: entrepreneurial opportunity recognition sits closer to human values and risk tolerance than most business-analysis tasks, and it is plausible the human contribution here proves more durable than a pure capability read would suggest.
MGT 2500.d: The Entrepreneurship BA program takes a student from idea discovery to business creation. In this course, students learn about entrepreneurship, the entrepreneurial mindset, and techniques to enhance creativity and innovative thinking. The course focuses on utilizing these tools and techniques to create venture solutions to address unmet needs, or identify opportunities, in stable and changing markets.

r: The course examines managerial functions and processes — planning, organizing, leading, and controlling — as they apply across business and other organizations. Much of the analytical and communicative work of management, including drafting plans, interpreting performance data, and producing reports, is exposed to AI, and observed-usage data shows management-related tasks as a rising share of current AI use. Management is also interpersonal, however, and AACSB accreditation supplies only a weak curricular lock rather than a course-specific mandate. At 24 months the rating is Medium: AI competently supports managerial analysis and drafting, partially eroding the instrumental case for this course, while near-term diffusion into everyday managerial practice and the course's interpersonal leadership content limit how far that erosion has actually progressed.

By 2031, AI will plausibly handle much of the analytical and communicative work of management — reporting, planning support, drafting, and data interpretation — and the applied tasks this course's knowledge serves will be broadly automatable. The interpersonal residue of actually leading and motivating people is real but represents a modest fraction of the course's total content, and AACSB's accreditation framework does not bind a specific course requirement. The rating rises to High: the applied managerial-knowledge work is performed competently by AI with limited human input for most of the course's content, Observed-usage growth in management-adjacent tasks and productivity studies showing large gains from AI-assisted drafting and analysis both point toward this broader erosion of the course's analytical content, even as the judgment involved in genuinely interpersonal and high-stakes managerial decisions remains where human managers concentrate their effort.

A decade out, AI is plausibly deeply embedded in managerial workflows, performing most analytical and administrative management work, with human managers focused on interpersonal leadership and contested judgment calls. The instrumental case for a course teaching general management functions as a body of personally-performed tasks is substantially eroded, shifting toward interpersonal and oversight competencies that represent a narrower slice of the syllabus. Capability-trend evidence on steadily lengthening AI task-time horizons makes this trajectory plausible well within the decade, even as macro-level diffusion research cautions that organizational adoption of such tools often lags raw capability. The rating is High, hedged by the durable interpersonal core of management work and by genuine ten-year uncertainty about capability and adoption. The direction is clear even so: the analytical bulk of what this course teaches automates, while the human-leadership residue persists without constituting the whole of the course.
MGT 3000.d: This course examines, analyzes, and assesses managerial functions and processes as related to business and other organizations. It is designed to prepare students to meet the challenges of a highly dynamic and ever-changing business environment by formulating individual competencies and skills, translating theory into practice, creating critical thinkers, and reflecting on the integration of new concepts and environmental changes into managerial practices.

r: The course has students research and develop a business concept, investigate market factors, plan financial strategies, and produce a business plan for a prospective venture. These are document-and-analysis-heavy tasks — market research synthesis, financial projection, business-plan drafting — that professional-writing productivity studies show AI already accelerates substantially while improving output quality, and observed-usage data confirms writing and analytical drafting as leading current-use categories. There is no embodiment, licensure, or institutional mandate protecting this elective entrepreneurship course, though it builds directly on MGT 2500. At 24 months the instrumental need is already meaningfully eroded for the drafting and research components, but near-term diffusion into how entrepreneurship instruction is actually delivered, and the course's role preparing students to think as founders, keep the rating at Medium rather than higher.

By 2031, AI business-planning and market-research tools will plausibly produce competent feasibility studies, financial projections, and venture business plans largely unassisted, and task-exposure research places this kind of analytical writing and quantitative estimation among more automatable activities. No embodiment, licensure, or accreditation floor constrains the course, and its foundational role is limited to a single prerequisite relationship rather than a load-bearing position across the curriculum. The rating rises to High: the applied feasibility-analysis and business-plan-drafting tasks the course teaches are broadly performable by AI with limited student input, Productivity research on AI-assisted professional writing shows substantial time savings paired with quality gains, a pattern that maps directly onto the drafting-heavy feasibility-study and business-plan work this course centers, even though the founder's underlying decision to pursue a given venture remains a human judgment call outside the course's task scope.

A decade out, AI systems will plausibly conduct much of the market research, financial modeling, and business-plan drafting this course currently teaches students to do by hand, with founders directing and validating rather than authoring these artifacts personally. The instrumental case for a course centered on personally producing a feasibility study is substantially eroded. Capability-trend research on lengthening AI task-time horizons makes this degree of automation plausible well before 2036, even though diffusion into how entrepreneurship programs actually teach the material may lag the underlying capability. The rating holds High, hedged by real uncertainty about how entrepreneurship education adapts — plausibly shifting toward evaluating AI-generated feasibility analyses and toward the judgment calls of actually committing capital and effort to a venture, competencies this course's current syllabus only partially addresses. No structural constraint pulls the rating back down at this horizon.
MGT 3020.d: Students examine the work of various entrepreneurs to gain insights into how new concepts are discovered and developed with particular emphasis on researching and developing a business concept, investigating market factors, planning financial strategies, and starting a business. Students are prepared to work on a business plan and also to be more creative managers.

r: The course covers business organizational forms, franchise arrangements, and government regulation of business including securities, antitrust, environmental, and bankruptcy law, alongside employment discrimination and labor law. This regulatory-compliance material spans several specialized legal domains where a plausible-looking but wrong answer carries real consequence — a mischaracterized securities exemption or bankruptcy priority rule is exactly the kind of confidently-wrong output that jagged-frontier research warns AI users are poorly calibrated to catch. That verification burden dampens the rating even though the underlying analytical work — reading regulations, summarizing compliance requirements — is a task category AI increasingly performs. Diffusion of specialized AI legal-compliance tools into everyday business regulatory practice also remains limited this early, reinforcing the near-term protection alongside the verification concern. At 24 months the instrumental need to build this specialized regulatory literacy personally remains intact, and the rating is Low.

By 2031, AI legal-research tools will plausibly handle routine regulatory summarization and compliance-question answering across securities, antitrust, and bankruptcy law fluently, and task-exposure research supports treating this document-centered analytical work as increasingly automatable. But the specialized, high-stakes character of these regulatory domains keeps a real verification burden in place: distinguishing a correct regulatory interpretation from a superficially plausible one still requires the trained human, particularly given documented AI legal-citation errors. Observed-usage data confirms document analysis and compliance-adjacent drafting as a growing share of professional AI use, supporting the shift toward AI-performed first-pass compliance work. That verification burden caps the erosion rather than eliminating the rating's rise. The rating moves to Medium: applied compliance-summarization tasks become largely AI-assisted, but the specialized regulatory judgment this course builds retains real instrumental value for catching AI errors in these domains.

A decade out, AI legal-compliance tools will plausibly be routine in business regulatory work, drafting and checking analyses across securities, antitrust, bankruptcy, and employment law with considerable fluency. Even so, these remain domains where an erroneous compliance judgment has serious legal and financial consequences, and the verification burden this course's specialized knowledge addresses does not disappear simply because AI drafts the first-pass analysis. Capability-trend evidence on lengthening AI task-time horizons makes broader competence across these specialized regulatory domains plausible by 2036, tempered by the same verification concern that constrains the rating at nearer horizons. The rating holds Medium, hedged by real uncertainty over how much regulatory-compliance work restructures around AI-assisted review versus how much retains a human-authored core. The central case has the course's instrumental value shifting from producing regulatory analysis to validating it, a real but not complete erosion of the original task rationale.
MGT 3220.d: This course provides an overview of the contemporary legal environment in which businesses operate. It explores various forms of business organizations, such as corporations and limited liability companies, and business opportunities, such as franchises. Also covered are important areas of government regulation of business including securities law, antitrust law, environmental law, and bankruptcy law. The course also delves into the realm of employment law, with a focus on employment discrimination, affirmative action, and labor law.

r: The course covers the legal context for international business decisions — customary law, treaties, import/export regulation, intellectual property, trade regulations, transportation, documentary transactions, and cross-border dispute resolution. Unlike domestic contract or tort law, this material spans fragmented and non-uniform legal systems where an AI system's confident answer may reflect one jurisdiction's rule presented as universal — exactly the miscalibrated-trust failure jagged-frontier research documents, and diffusion of specialized cross-jurisdictional legal AI tools into routine practice remains limited this early. That combination of higher verification burden and slower near-term diffusion keeps exposure lower than for general business law at this horizon. At 24 months the instrumental need to build this cross-jurisdictional legal literacy personally is essentially intact, and the rating is Low.

By 2031, AI legal-research tools will be meaningfully better at synthesizing cross-jurisdictional rules, treaty provisions, and international trade-regulation questions, narrowing the gap with domestic legal-analysis tasks that task-exposure research already treats as more exposed. But the fragmented, non-uniform character of international commercial law — different jurisdictions, differing treaty adherence, dispute-resolution forums — sustains a real verification burden that a single querying pass does not resolve, keeping the rating capped. The rating stays Low: international legal analysis is harder to automate reliably than domestic business law given the diversity of governing regimes involved, and Observed-usage growth in document analysis and cross-border business tasks supports treating the underlying research work as increasingly exposed, even as the fragmented-jurisdiction verification concern holds the rating down and the course's specialized cross-border literacy remains instrumentally necessary for catching AI's jurisdiction-blending errors in this specific domain.

A decade out, AI legal-analysis tools will plausibly handle much cross-jurisdictional research competently, including treaty interpretation and international trade-regulation summarization, as capability growth compounds across specialized legal domains. The instrumental case for personally performing this analytical work erodes meaningfully at this longer horizon, even though the fragmented-jurisdiction verification burden that protected the course at nearer horizons persists in weaker form. Capability-trend research on lengthening AI task-time horizons supports extrapolating meaningful gains in cross-jurisdictional legal synthesis by 2036, though diffusion into specialized international-practice settings plausibly lags the underlying capability curve. The rating rises to Medium, hedged substantially: international law's non-uniformity is a genuinely hard problem for any single AI system to resolve reliably across all relevant jurisdictions, and it is plausible the verification burden proves more durable over the decade than this rating's central case assumes.
MGT 3230.d: This course covers the legal context for international business decisions. Topics include selected elements of international law such as customary law and the law of treaties. Also covered are the international law of important/exporting, intellectual property, trade regulations, transportation, documentary transactions, contracts, agency/employment, and dispute resolution. Ethical aspects of the above areas are discussed.

r: The course studies statutory, common-law, and constitutional employment and HR law with a practical emphasis on Colorado and federal antidiscrimination rules, labor law, litigation prevention, and privacy. This is exactly the kind of compliance-document analysis that is highly exposed in principle — observed-usage data shows business-and-legal drafting rising as an AI-use category — but employment-discrimination and litigation-prevention judgments carry serious liability exposure, and a superficially reasonable but wrong compliance answer is the confidently-miscalibrated failure mode jagged-frontier research warns about. That verification burden dampens the near-term rating even as the underlying analytical work is automatable in principle. Diffusion of AI-assisted HR-compliance platforms into everyday employer practice also remains uneven this early, reinforcing the near-term protection alongside the verification concern. At 24 months the instrumental need to build this practical compliance literacy personally is intact, and the rating is Low.

By 2031, AI HR-compliance tools will plausibly draft policy language, flag discrimination risk, and summarize labor-law obligations with real fluency, and task-exposure research supports treating this document-centered compliance work as increasingly automatable. The litigation-prevention stakes and privacy considerations at the center of the course keep a genuine verification burden in place, since an AI-drafted compliance judgment that misses a Colorado-specific wrinkle or a recent case development creates real liability exposure that only a knowledgeable human catches. Observed-usage data confirms compliance-adjacent document drafting as a growing share of professional AI use, supporting the shift toward AI-performed first-pass employment-law analysis at this horizon. That burden caps rather than reverses the erosion. The rating moves to Medium: routine compliance drafting and summarization become largely AI-performed, while the practical legal judgment this course builds retains real instrumental value in reviewing that output.

A decade out, AI compliance tools will plausibly be routine in HR and employment-law practice, drafting policy language and flagging discrimination or labor-law risk with considerable competence. Even so, employment litigation carries serious financial and reputational consequences, and the verification burden this course addresses — catching a wrong or jurisdictionally stale compliance judgment before it becomes a lawsuit — does not disappear merely because AI produces the first draft. Capability-trend evidence on lengthening AI task-time horizons makes broader competence in employment-law compliance work plausible by 2036, tempered by the same liability-driven verification concern that anchors the rating at nearer horizons. The rating holds Medium, hedged by uncertainty about how much employment-law practice restructures around AI-assisted compliance review versus retaining a human-authored analytical core, and by the practical, Colorado-specific emphasis of the course, which plausibly sustains more durable human involvement than a general capability read would suggest.
MGT 3240.d: This course is an in-depth study of the legal and practical implications of employment and human resources law. Students interested in management, human resources or owning their own business will benefit from this course. Topics include statutory law, common law and constitutional law as it relates to the employment/human resources context, employer/ employee relationship, antidiscrimination laws, labor law, litigation prevention methods and privacy. The focus of the course is on the practical elements of law, with an emphasis on Colorado and federal law.

r: The course surveys Colorado's prior-appropriation water law and water-rights administration, including the state's climate, geology, and hydrology context, the administrative processes governing water distribution, and the policy considerations shaping allocation decisions. This is deeply jurisdiction-specific regulatory content — Colorado water-court doctrine, decree administration, augmentation-plan practice — far narrower and less represented in general training data than mainstream contract or tort law, which plausibly leaves general-purpose AI tools less reliable here than in more common legal domains. Diffusion of specialized water-law AI tools into Colorado administrative practice is negligible at this horizon. Task-exposure research's finding that critical-thinking-intensive work resists automation applies with particular force to this kind of hydrology-dependent, fact-specific administrative reasoning. At 24 months the instrumental need to build this niche regulatory-administrative literacy personally is essentially intact, and the rating is Low.

By 2031, general AI legal-research capability will have grown substantially, but the niche, state-specific character of Colorado water administration — augmentation plans, water-court procedure, prior-appropriation priority disputes — is exactly the kind of thinly-represented specialized domain where jagged-frontier research's caution about miscalibrated trust applies most acutely: a plausible-sounding but wrong answer on priority dates or decree conditions carries real economic and legal consequence for agricultural and municipal water users. Diffusion of AI tools purpose-built for this administrative niche remains limited even at this horizon. Macro-level diffusion research on uneven AI adoption across firms and agencies supports treating specialized state-administrative practice as a laggard rather than a leader in this technology transition. The rating stays Low: the specialized, jurisdiction-bound nature of the subject matter resists the general erosion pattern seen in broader business-law coursework, and the course's practical administrative literacy remains instrumentally necessary.

A decade out, AI capability will be considerably stronger across even niche legal-administrative domains, and it is plausible that Colorado water-rights research and administrative-filing support become meaningfully AI-assisted by 2036. But the underlying task — reasoning through prior-appropriation priority, hydrology-dependent allocation disputes, and state-specific administrative procedure under real economic stakes — remains a specialized, high-verification-burden domain where an erroneous conclusion has direct consequences for water users. Capability-trend evidence on lengthening AI task-time horizons still supports meaningful gains in specialized legal-administrative reasoning by 2036, but adoption diffusion into a niche, state-specific practice area plausibly lags the general trend. The rating holds Low, with the acknowledged uncertainty that broad capability growth could erode this niche faster than the central case assumes; but the combination of jurisdictional specificity and administrative consequence keeps this course among the more durably necessary in the business-law family through 2036.
MGT 3250.d: This course provides students with an in-depth study of the unique nature of Colorado water law and Colorado water rights administration. The course will survey the key issues surrounding the legal framework governing the allocation of water resources, administrative processes affecting water distribution, and policy considerations that influence decisions about the use and management of water resources in the state of Colorado. An overview of Colorado climate, geology and hydrology, as well as a review of Colorado's early water use and development will provide the context for the study of the legal system with which the state and its citizens allocate water.

r: MGT 3260 trains students to identify property, liability, and operational risk, evaluate loss exposure, and design risk-retention or risk-transfer strategies, including legal considerations and risk-financing choices. These tasks map to analyzing data or information and evaluating information against compliance standards, activities inside the Computer and Mathematical category the Anthropic Economic Index identifies as the largest observed-usage share, and task-exposure research classifies quantitative analytical writing as strongly positively exposed. Drafting loss projections and risk-financing memos is already assisted by generative tools. At 24 months, however, Census BTOS diffusion data show only a minority of firms have deployed such workflows, and legal-consideration content still needs a knowledgeable human check before a risk strategy is adopted. The rating is Medium: analytical risk work is meaningfully AI-assisted but not yet fully substituted, and AACSB accreditation exerts no course-specific lock.

By 2031, AI systems will competently perform the bulk of risk-identification, loss-quantification, and risk-financing-option analysis that this course teaches, drawing on the same analytical and evaluative work activities that already dominate observed enterprise usage. Productivity research on professional writing shows large quality and time gains on document-heavy analytical tasks, which describes much of a risk plan's construction. Verification burden remains moderate rather than protective — a competent generalist can check a risk memo without deep specialist training — and there is no embodiment or licensure constraint on the content. With diffusion assumed to broaden considerably over five years, the applied instrumental work of identifying, evaluating, and structuring business risk becomes largely automatable, and the course's knowledge is substantially, though not completely, performed by AI rather than by the student who has taken it. The rating is High.

A decade out, capability trends compound: METR-style task-horizon growth implies systems handling substantially longer, more open-ended analytical assignments than five-year-out tools, and risk identification, quantification, and financing-strategy design are exactly the kind of multi-step analytical task that benefits from that trajectory. AACSB provides no course-specific mandate to anchor the course against this trend, and nothing about property, liability, or operational risk analysis is physically embodied or real-time interpersonal. The rating is High, but held with appropriate hedging: ten-year capability and diffusion forecasts carry real uncertainty, and legal or regulatory shifts in how risk decisions must be documented and attributed to a human could re-introduce verification requirements not visible from today's vantage point. The central-case trajectory nonetheless points toward broad, if not complete, automatability of the course's applied work.
MGT 3260.d: This course addresses how business owners/managers deal with the various risks of running a business. Businesses can face unexpected and accidental losses from a variety of sources and, without a solid risk management plan for these contingencies, the resulting losses can result in bankruptcy. This course focuses on the processes used in identifying risk, evaluating the potential for losses to the organization, and creating a strategy to retain or transfer the risk. Major topics include risk to property, liability risk, legal considerations, risk financing strategies, and operational and strategic risks.

r: This course centers on relationship management among nonprofit staff, board members, volunteers, and clients, plus self-assessment of a student's own interpersonal strengths and career strategy. The applied work — building trust with a volunteer, negotiating board expectations, coaching a struggling staff member — sits in the real-time interpersonal and coaching-and-developing-others activities that task-exposure research consistently finds negatively associated with AI exposure relative to programming or drafting work. Some administrative content, like summarizing nonprofit regulations, is assisted by generative tools, but the course's instrumental core is relational judgment exercised with specific people over time, not information production. At 24 months the rating is Low: AI can support background research, but it does not perform the relationship-building work this course exists to teach, and AACSB accreditation imposes no offsetting mandate.

By 2031, AI assistants will likely draft board memos, summarize volunteer-management best practices, and organize regulatory compliance information faster than a student can today, nudging the analytical periphery of this course toward automation. But the applied tasks that give the course its instrumental purpose — coaching staff, resolving conflict among board and volunteers, reading a client's needs in person — remain interpersonal and low-exposure by the same research classifying such work as resistant. Observed-usage data still shows office and writing tasks as the automated slice, not relationship management itself. The verification burden is moderate rather than protective, but embodiment and real-time human presence keep this at Low, hedged only slightly upward from 24 months because the administrative surround continues to thin without touching the relational substance.

Ten years out, genuine uncertainty widens. Capability trend evidence (METR/Epoch task-horizon doubling) suggests systems handling much longer and more socially complex tasks than today, and it is plausible some coached interactions could be partially mediated by AI tools that draft talking points or triage volunteer communications. That incremental shift nudges the rating to Medium at ten years — a hedge, not a confident prediction — because the course's substrate is still relationship management with staff, board, volunteers, and clients, an interpersonal activity that task-exposure research treats as durably low-exposure even as adjacent administrative work automates further. No licensure or accreditation mandate anchors the course against this drift; the protection comes entirely from the embodied, real-time nature of the work itself, which is why the rating rises only one band rather than to High.
MGT 3510.d: In this course, students examine the human capital component of the nonprofit sphere. Roles, responsibilities, rules, and regulations are all explored as they relate to self, staff, board members, volunteers, clients and outside agency partners. Students explore their unique strengths and build respective strategies to employ throughout their careers.

r: MGT 3530 covers recruitment, selection, performance appraisal, and compensation, and in some sections has students work directly with a business client. Screening resumes, drafting job postings, structuring compensation benchmarks, and producing first-draft appraisal language are analytical, writing-heavy activities that observed usage data already shows concentrated in the largest AI-usage category, and generative tools are visibly present in recruiting workflows today. But hiring and appraisal decisions carry real legal exposure under discrimination and labor law, and the course's client-engagement component involves live human interaction that a knowledgeable instructor still supervises. That mix of exposed administrative tasks and legally consequential interpersonal judgment keeps the 24-month rating at Medium: the instrumental case is eroding for the paperwork side of HR faster than for the judgment side, with AACSB imposing no offsetting mandate.

By 2031, AI will plausibly handle the large majority of HR's document production and analytical benchmarking — resume screening, compensation modeling, appraisal drafting — with productivity research on professional writing tasks (large time savings, quality gains) as the closest available analogue. The psychological, social, legal, and economic bases the course teaches remain necessary for a human to interpret correctly, but the applied instrumental work of producing HR documents and analyses is substantially automatable by this horizon, and no licensure or accreditation floor protects the course. The rating moves to High: the jagged-frontier finding that AI users are less accurate on tasks outside a system's competence argues some human legal review persists, but that residual is a minority of the applied work the course covers.

A decade out, HR administrative and analytical work — staffing decisions, compensation structuring, performance documentation — is plausibly deeply AI-mediated given the capability trajectory (METR/Epoch task-horizon growth) and the category's already-high observed usage. Client-facing engagement and legally consequential judgment calls are the most durable residual, but they represent a shrinking share of what the course's syllabus actually covers, and the psychological and social bases the course teaches would migrate toward oversight of AI-drafted personnel decisions rather than disappearing outright. AACSB's accreditation framework still imposes no course-specific mandate to anchor this against drift. The rating holds at High, hedged: ten-year forecasts of both capability and diffusion carry genuine uncertainty, and labor and employment law could evolve to require documented human sign-off on AI-assisted personnel decisions, which would preserve more human involvement in HR practice than a pure capability trend alone would predict.
MGT 3530.d: This course provides the student with a broad overview of the contemporary issues, theories, and principles used to effectively manage human resources in organizations. The psychological, social, legal, and economic bases underlying the practices of human resource management are studied. Topics such as recruitment, selection, performance appraisal, and compensation are analyzed. Some sections of this course are taught with an actual business client. Students engage with the client in conjunction with classroom learning.

r: This course teaches quantitative decision-making for production and service systems — capacity, layout, location, forecasting, quality control, inventory, and project management — with special emphasis on quantitative technique. These are archetypal analyzing-data-or-information and scheduling-work-and-activities tasks, and the Computer and Mathematical category the Anthropic Economic Index identifies as the largest usage share covers exactly this kind of modeling and forecasting work. Optimization and forecasting tools already assist much of this analysis today. At 24 months, though, BTOS diffusion data show only a minority of firms have operationalized such AI-driven planning broadly, and the rating stays at Medium: the quantitative technique this course teaches is highly exposed in principle but not yet fully deployed across the operations functions it targets, with AACSB imposing no course-specific constraint.

By 2031, forecasting, capacity planning, quality-control analysis, and inventory optimization are plausible candidates for broad AI competence and deployment, since this is quantitative technique work squarely inside the largest observed-usage category and the type of structured analytical task where productivity research (e.g., large speed gains on technical, code-like tasks such as those measured with GitHub Copilot) shows the biggest measured gains. Verification burden is moderate — outputs are checkable against operational data rather than requiring adversarial specialist review — and nothing about the content is physically embodied or real-time interpersonal. With no licensure or foundational-course constraint in play, the applied work the course teaches becomes largely automatable at this horizon. The rating is High, reflecting substantial confidence that operations-planning technique diffuses broadly across production and service organizations by 2031.

Ten years out, capability-trend evidence (METR/Epoch task-horizon doubling roughly every four to seven months) implies operations-planning problems of considerably greater length and complexity than today's tools handle competently, covering forecasting, layout and location decisions, and supply-chain-adjacent scheduling together rather than piecemeal, and integrating them with broader organizational strategy in a way current tools cannot yet match. The course's quantitative technique orientation offers little embodied or interpersonal residue to resist this trend, and AACSB accreditation remains a weak lock rather than a course-specific mandate. The rating holds at High, hedged for the horizon: macro-diffusion evidence suggests real-economy productivity effects remain modest even as capability grows, so some operations functions may still rely on human planners where organizational adoption lags the technical frontier, tempering full certainty about the ten-year outcome.
MGT 3550.d: This course is an introduction to operations management decision-making and to the tools used to enhance the decision-making process. Attention is given to the design and operation of the production/service system and its interrelationship with other systems in the organization. The course places special emphasis on the use of quantitative techniques in decision making. Topics include productivity, strategic positioning and design of operations (e.g., capacity, layout, location, and work methods), project management, forecasting, quality control, supply-chain management, and inventory management.

r: MGT 3720 teaches a stakeholder-based strategic framework — how adopting an expansive stakeholder view builds competitive advantage and increases both social impact and profitability. The applied work is strategic writing and analysis: assessing stakeholder impact, articulating a sustainability-linked strategy, and communicating it to peers and supervisors, all of which fall under developing-objectives-and-strategies and are the kind of writing task that observed AI usage already concentrates around. GDPval evidence shows current frontier models approaching but not yet matching human experts on real strategic deliverables. At 24 months, the rating is Medium: AI meaningfully assists stakeholder analysis and strategy drafting, but the applied output is not yet reliably at expert parity, and AACSB imposes no course-specific mandate to hold the rating down further.

By 2031, competitive-advantage and stakeholder-strategy analysis of the kind this course teaches is plausibly well within reach of AI systems that draft, critique, and structure strategic arguments competently, building on the GDPval trajectory toward parity with human experts on real deliverables and on productivity research showing large quality gains on professional writing tasks. The verification burden is moderate rather than protective — a business audience can assess whether a stakeholder strategy is internally coherent without deep specialist training — and nothing in the content is embodied or real-time interpersonal in the protective sense the rubric treats as durable. With no licensure or foundational-course constraint, the rating moves to High: the applied strategic-writing and stakeholder-impact-assessment work the course teaches is substantially automatable, if not fully complete, by this horizon.

A decade out, the capability trajectory (METR/Epoch task-horizon growth) points toward AI competently handling longer, more integrative strategic-analysis assignments than a single stakeholder memo, weaving sustainability, stakeholder impact, and financial-return arguments into one coherent strategy document — which is the direction this course's applied work would need to resist to stay protected, and no institutional lock does that resisting for it. AACSB accreditation remains a weak, non-course-specific constraint. The rating holds at High, but with real hedging: ten-year forecasts of both capability and organizational diffusion carry substantial uncertainty, and the macro-productivity evidence (Acemoglu's modest ten-year TFP estimate) suggests economy-wide adoption of AI-driven strategy work could lag the technical frontier considerably, leaving some genuine but shrinking role for human-authored stakeholder strategy.
MGT 3720.d: Firms are recognizing the importance of sustainability and in response are adopting an expansive stakeholder view as a way to acquire a competitive advantage and increase financial returns. This course describes how a stakeholder perspective impacts all areas of a firm. The course also describes how a stakeholder view of strategy can create a "conscious company" that provides a positive impact to society and the environment while also increasing profitability.

r: This survey course covers trade barriers, cultural differences, foreign-market entry strategies, currency exposure, and political and economic environments — knowledge-synthesis work mapping to getting information and interpreting the meaning of information for others. Summarizing country-risk factors, comparing entry-mode options, and drafting market-entry briefs are the kind of research-and-writing tasks that observed AI usage data already shows concentrated in the largest usage category, and current tools handle broad informational synthesis competently today. At 24 months, though, BTOS diffusion evidence shows deployment still uneven across firms, and cross-cultural judgment about how findings apply to a specific market retains a meaningful human role. The rating is Medium: the informational synthesis this course builds is already substantially AI-assisted, without full displacement yet, and AACSB provides no course-specific lock.

By 2031, AI systems will plausibly perform most of the informational synthesis this course covers — trade-barrier analysis, currency and political-risk summaries, comparative entry-strategy evaluation — competently and at scale, consistent with task-exposure research finding writing and analytical-synthesis work strongly positively exposed, and with observed-usage data already showing such research-and-writing tasks concentrated in the largest AI-usage category. Verification burden is moderate: an instructor or manager can sanity-check a market-entry brief without deep specialist expertise, so it does not offer strong protection. Nothing in the course content is embodied, and no licensure or foundational-course role constrains it. The rating moves to High: the applied instrumental task of synthesizing international-business information becomes broadly automatable, even as genuine strategic judgment about which market to enter remains a smaller residual.

Ten years out, the capability trend (METR/Epoch task-horizon doubling) suggests AI handling considerably more integrative cross-border analysis than five-year-out tools, folding trade, currency, cultural, and political factors into a single coherent assessment rather than separate summaries, and drafting complete market-entry strategies rather than component briefs. AACSB remains a weak lock that does nothing to anchor this course against the trend, and nothing about international-business analysis is physically embodied or real-time interpersonal in a way the rubric treats as protective. The rating holds at High, hedged appropriately: macro-adoption evidence (Acemoglu's modest ten-year TFP estimate) suggests real organizational uptake could lag the technical frontier, and geopolitical volatility over a decade could keep some human political-risk judgment in demand even as the analytical baseline underneath it is thoroughly AI-performed.
MGT 3820.d: This course is designed to enhance understanding of the international environment faced by businesses. Trade barriers, cultural differences, entry strategies into foreign markets, foreign currency, political environments, and economic environments are among the many topics surveyed to assist students in becoming aware of international issues and events influencing management in today's global environment.

r: Students in MGT 3850 compare entrepreneurial conditions across countries and produce a feasibility plan for an international venture — a deliverable combining country-comparison research, market analysis, and structured business-plan writing. That maps directly to developing-objectives-and-strategies and documenting/recording information, both concentrated in the Computer and Mathematical and writing-heavy activities the Anthropic Economic Index flags as the largest observed-usage categories. Generative tools already draft feasibility-plan sections and compile comparative country data competently, and task-exposure research classifies this kind of comparative analytical writing as strongly positively exposed. GDPval evidence shows current models approaching but not yet matching expert-level real deliverables, which keeps genuine judgment about venture viability partly human for now. At 24 months the rating is Medium: the feasibility-plan drafting task is heavily AI-assisted without full substitution, and AACSB imposes no course-specific constraint.

By 2031, producing a structured feasibility plan — country comparison, market-entry analysis, venture justification — is plausibly within reach of AI systems performing at or near the standard this course currently asks of students, extending the GDPval trajectory toward expert parity on real occupational deliverables and consistent with productivity research showing large gains on professional-writing tasks. Verification burden remains moderate rather than protective: a feasibility plan can be checked by a non-specialist instructor or advisor rather than requiring deep domain expertise. Nothing in the content is embodied or real-time interpersonal, and no licensure or foundational-course role protects it. The rating moves to High: the instrumental work of researching and drafting an international feasibility plan becomes broadly automatable at this horizon, even if not completely.

A decade out, capability-trend evidence (METR/Epoch task-horizon doubling) suggests AI handling considerably more open-ended entrepreneurial planning than a single feasibility document, integrating market research, financial projection, and strategic framing end to end into a single coherent venture proposal spanning multiple candidate countries at once. AACSB accreditation remains a weak, non-binding lock on this content, and nothing about comparative venture analysis is physically embodied or real-time interpersonal. The rating holds at High, hedged for genuine ten-year uncertainty: macro-diffusion evidence indicates real-economy AI adoption could lag the technical frontier by a wide margin, and entrepreneurial judgment about which of several AI-generated venture concepts is actually worth pursuing plausibly stays a human function even as the drafting and comparative-research work underneath it is thoroughly automated.
MGT 3850.d: This course focuses on opportunities for starting and developing new ventures in parts of the world outside the U.S. Characteristics that influence entrepreneurship in select countries, whose cultures and income levels are vastly different from one another, are examined, requiring students to compare, contrast, and draw conclusions about new venture opportunities in those countries. Students will develop a feasibility plan for an international venture opportunity in a selected foreign market. Upon completing this course, students will have a better understanding of the unique elements associated with starting a new venture in a foreign country.

r: MGT 3860 is a compact overview course teaching students to identify unmet social needs and analyze their potential for solution through a viable social enterprise — needs-identification and objective-development work close to getting information and developing objectives and strategies. Drafting a social-need analysis or a viability assessment is the kind of research-and-writing task already assisted by generative tools, consistent with the Anthropic Economic Index finding writing and analytical tasks prominent in observed usage. The course description is brief relative to others in this batch, which limits how precisely its applied tasks can be mapped, but the content that is described is squarely knowledge-work rather than embodied or licensure-bound. At 24 months the rating is Medium: the analytical core is meaningfully AI-assisted without full displacement, and AACSB imposes no course-specific constraint.

By 2031, identifying unmet social needs and assessing enterprise viability — essentially structured problem-framing and feasibility analysis — is plausibly well within AI competence, extending today's already-visible assistance with market and needs research and consistent with task-exposure research's finding that analytical synthesis work is strongly exposed, alongside observed-usage data placing such research-and-writing tasks in the largest AI-usage category. Verification burden is moderate, not protective: a viability assessment can be reviewed without deep specialist training. Nothing in the sparse course description points to embodiment, licensure, or a foundational role protecting it against this trajectory. The rating moves to High, though confidence stays lower than for more detailed courses in this batch because the brief description leaves some of the applied task mix underspecified.

Ten years out, the same capability-trend logic (METR/Epoch task-horizon growth) that applies across this batch's analytical, non-embodied courses applies here: AI plausibly performs sophisticated social-needs analysis and venture-viability assessment as a matter of course, integrating market research and financial framing that today requires separate steps. AACSB remains a weak lock that does not anchor this content against the trend, and nothing about need-identification analysis is physically embodied. The rating holds at High, hedged more than usual given the course description's brevity — the precise mix of creative, human-centered problem-framing versus formulaic viability analysis is not fully specified, and genuine judgment about which social problems are worth an enterprise response could retain more human involvement than the analytical baseline alone would suggest.
MGT 3860.d: This course provides an overview of social entrepreneurship, explains the skills required to identify unmet social needs and analyze their potential for solution with a viable social enterprise.

r: MGT 3980 places a student, under faculty supervision, into a real professional placement arranged through the Classroom to Career Hub, with requirements varying by department. The applied work is whatever the host organization assigns, but the course's instrumental purpose is the supervised, in-person experience itself — coordinating with supervisors and peers, performing real administrative activities, and building workplace judgment under live conditions — which is real-time and presence-dependent rather than a discrete deliverable an AI system could substitute for. Task-exposure research consistently finds embodied, interpersonal placement work low-exposure relative to drafting or analysis. At 24 months the rating is Low: individual tasks within an internship may be AI-assisted, but the supervised-placement experience the course exists to certify is not something an AI performs on the student's behalf.

By 2031, AI assistants will likely help interns draft memos, summarize meetings, and analyze data faster inside whatever function they are placed in, consistent with observed-usage data showing office and writing tasks heavily automated already. But the course's instrumental core is not the specific deliverables produced during the placement — it is the supervised, embodied experience of functioning inside a real organization, coordinating with real supervisors and peers, that the internship certifies. That protective embodiment does not fully hold at this horizon given how much of the surrounding task content is exposed, so the rating rises to Medium: the work an intern does is increasingly AI-assisted even as the requirement to be supervised in a real placement persists unchanged, with AACSB again imposing no course-specific lock either way.

Ten years out, genuine uncertainty compounds: if internship placements themselves evolve toward AI-mediated or remote-hybrid work as capability and diffusion both grow (METR/Epoch capability trend; Census BTOS adoption still uneven at present), the embodied protection this course currently relies on could weaken somewhat, though the faculty-supervised, real-organization placement structure itself is not something a catalog requirement removes quickly, and management functions still typically require a designated organizational sponsor for a student to work under. The rating holds at Medium, hedged: the tasks an intern performs day-to-day are plausibly substantially automated by 2036, but the course's requirement of supervised presence inside an actual employer relationship, documented and certified by a faculty member, is a structural feature that resists the same erosion applying to discrete analytical deliverables elsewhere in this batch.
MGT 3980.d: Supervised by a faculty member within the major department, internships provide practical, hands-on experience in a professional field related to the major. Internship placements must be established prior to enrollment in this course in consultation with the Classroom to Career (C2) Hub. Internship requirements vary by department. For information and instructions on finding and enrolling in an internship, contact the Classroom to Career (C2) Hub at [contact omitted].

r: MGT 4050 covers the full supply-chain sequence — forecasting, demand management, sourcing and procurement, sales and operations planning, and logistics — introducing quantitative models as needed, and ties it to overall business strategy. Demand forecasting, sourcing analysis, and logistics optimization are analyzing-data-or-information and scheduling-work-and-activities tasks that fall inside the Computer and Mathematical category the Anthropic Economic Index identifies as the largest observed-usage share, and supply-chain planning software already embeds substantial automated forecasting and optimization. At 24 months, BTOS diffusion data show only a minority of firms have deployed AI-driven planning broadly across these functions, and the strategic role of supply chain within the firm still needs human framing. The rating is Medium: the quantitative technique is highly exposed but not yet broadly deployed, with AACSB imposing no course-specific mandate.

By 2031, forecasting, sourcing analysis, and logistics-network optimization are plausibly performed competently by AI at scale, consistent with the strongly positive exposure task-exposure research assigns to quantitative analytical work and with productivity research showing large gains on structured technical tasks. Verification burden is moderate: supply-chain outputs are checkable against operational and financial data rather than requiring deep adversarial review, so it offers limited protection. Nothing in the content is physically embodied, and no licensure or foundational-course constraint applies. The rating moves to High: the applied instrumental work — demand forecasting, sourcing decisions, logistics planning — the course teaches becomes largely automatable by this horizon, even as strategic framing of supply chain's role in the firm remains a smaller human residual.

Ten years out, capability-trend evidence (METR/Epoch task-horizon doubling roughly every four to seven months) points toward AI systems integrating forecasting, sourcing, and logistics into unified end-to-end supply-chain decisions rather than the piecemeal analysis of today, extending the course's already-high exposure further and tying it more directly to the overall business strategy the course emphasizes. AACSB accreditation remains a weak lock that does not anchor this content against the trend. The rating holds at High, hedged: macro-diffusion evidence (Acemoglu's modest ten-year TFP estimate) suggests real organizational adoption across global, often legacy-system-dependent supply chains could lag the technical frontier meaningfully, and geopolitical or logistics disruptions over a decade could keep some human strategic judgment in demand even as the analytical baseline is thoroughly AI-performed.
MGT 4050.d: This course covers contemporary supply chain issues, concepts, and techniques. Supply Chain Management (SCM) is a cross-functional discipline concerned with the movement of products, the use of business resources, the flow of information, and the deployment of services in the value chain. In this introductory course to SCM, students are provided with a comprehensive overview of business processes, value creating activities, and best practices for a supply chain - from forecasting and demand management, to sourcing and procurement, to sales and operations planning, and through logistics (i.e., warehousing, distribution, and transportation), out to the customer. The course covers both the tactical and strategic perspectives of SCM and is based on supply chain operations in the real world. Quantitative models are introduced as needed. The course pinpoints the role of supply chain in the overall business strategy of the firm and its relationship to other functional areas of the firm.

r: This course applies analytical tools to service operations: designing the service delivery system, managing capacity, running scheduling and queueing analysis, setting yield-management policy, and evaluating productivity and quality, alongside adopting new information technologies. These are largely quantitative, optimization-style tasks that already run through specialized software, and observed-usage data shows the Computer and Mathematical category as the single largest share of AI use, overlapping directly with this analytical core. Firm-level diffusion of AI tools into operations planning is real but still uneven at this horizon, and there is no licensure gate here, only a weak AACSB-level curricular lock. At 24 months the instrumental need to learn queueing analysis and capacity modeling manually is already softening as tools mature, but firms have not yet restructured service-operations roles enough to erase the requirement. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI tools will competently generate capacity plans, staffing schedules, and yield-management recommendations from operational data, and the capability-trend evidence on rapid gains in task-time horizons supports broad deployment across this material by then. The course's applied tasks sit squarely inside highly exposed analytical work, and nothing structural protects it: the delivery-system design and queueing calculations the course teaches are executable by AI with limited human input for routine cases. The weak AACSB lock does not bind, and there is no foundational role holding the course back from a higher rating. The residual is judging when an automated recommendation misreads an unusual service context, a real but narrower competence than the full course content. Rating rises to High, reflecting the same forces that erode principles-of-marketing-style analytical business courses.

A decade out, the central case has AI systems performing most routine service-operations analysis and recommendation end to end, with human planners concentrated on unusual demand patterns, novel service concepts, and cross-functional judgment calls that resist templated optimization. The instrumental case for a course teaching manual queueing and capacity techniques is substantially eroded under this trajectory. The rating holds High, hedged by real uncertainty about how quickly individual service firms actually restructure planning roles around automated tools versus keeping human planners as a check on edge cases. Confidence is moderate rather than high because the course description names techniques rather than a specific occupational deliverable, making the ten-year mapping somewhat more approximate than for courses with a sharper task profile, and because the pace of firm-level adoption over a full decade is itself genuinely uncertain.
MGT 4360.d: This course covers the concepts and analytical tools required for understanding and managing service operations. Specifically, the course addresses issues in planning, designing, analyzing and controlling a service production system in the area of development of service concept and operations strategy, design of service delivery system, capacity management, service scheduling/queueing analysis, yield management, productivity and quality evaluation and management, and the use of new information technologies.

r: Students here prepare a comprehensive business plan covering market analysis, competitive assessment, workforce and capacity planning, and financial viability, packaged to attract seed and growth capital. This is a document-production and analytical-synthesis task closely aligned with the professional-writing evidence base, where controlled studies show AI assistance cutting drafting time substantially while raising quality. Market-analysis sections and financial projections are already assemble-able from AI-generated research and templates. There is no licensure lock and only a weak AACSB-level constraint on the course's existence; it also feeds directly into the entrepreneurship capstone taken concurrently, giving it a modest curricular link rather than deep foundational weight. At 24 months the instrumental need to hand-draft a full plan is measurably reduced but not gone, since investors and instructors still expect a coherent human-directed strategic narrative. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI tools will competently draft market analyses, financial projections, and full business-plan sections on request, and productivity research on professional writing — large time savings paired with quality gains — extends naturally to this genre of persuasive, structured business document. The applied work the course teaches, generating and packaging the plan, is broadly automatable, and neither the weak AACSB lock nor the light link to the capstone course is strong enough to hold the rating down. What remains distinctly human is framing a venture's strategic logic and negotiating with investors, a narrower slice of the course's content than the drafting work itself. Rating rises to High, tracking the same erosion seen in other document-heavy business courses once near-term diffusion limits fall away.

A decade out, the central case has AI producing investor-ready business plans essentially on demand, including market sizing, competitive positioning, and financial modeling, leaving founders to supply the underlying venture idea and to defend it in negotiation. The instrumental case for a course centered on manually assembling the plan document is substantially eroded under this trajectory. The rating holds High, with a genuine hedge: business-plan quality is judged partly on investor trust in the founding team's own command of the material, which could sustain more hands-on plan-writing pedagogy than a pure capability read implies. The uncertainty is about how planning pedagogy adapts under ubiquitous AI drafting tools, not about whether the drafting task itself remains AI-resistant over this horizon, which the broader evidence base does not support.
MGT 4420.d: Students learn how to prepare a definitive, comprehensive business plan involving all aspects of a proposed new venture. To attract seed money and growth capital, the business plan must address probable start-up issues involving market analysis, competition, workforce and capacity planning. Emphasis is on financial viability and business plan packaging to secure financial seed money.

r: As the entrepreneurship capstone, this course covers the tasks of launching a startup venture, growing it past the startup stage, and managing it toward survival, growth, or exit. Much of this is analytical and planning work — market and financial assessment, growth-strategy formulation — that overlaps the business-analysis tasks observed-usage data places within the largest AI-use category, but running an actual venture also involves messy, ambiguous, real-time decisions about people and operations that resist clean automation. There is no licensure or gen-ed lock, and as a terminal capstone nothing downstream depends on it. At 24 months, AI assists planning and analysis substantially, but the entrepreneurial judgment under genuine uncertainty that the course centers on remains squarely a student's own to develop. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI will competently support most of the analytical scaffolding around running a venture — financial modeling, market monitoring, operational reporting — but the jagged-frontier evidence is directly relevant here: founders operating outside a model's reliable zone, in the genuinely novel situations that define startup survival and growth decisions, risk material errors from over-trusting AI recommendations. That verification tension is real, yet it does not rise to the level of a strong institutional cap, and the course's terminal, capstone position means no foundational-scaffolding constraint holds it down either. The rating rises to High: the bulk of the applied planning and analysis work is broadly automatable, even as founder-level judgment under ambiguity remains a genuine and only partially delegable residue.

A decade out, AI-assisted venture planning, operations monitoring, and even much exit-strategy analysis will be routine, and the instrumental case for a course teaching students to perform these tasks by hand is substantially eroded in the central case. What plausibly persists is the founder's own capacity to make high-stakes, ambiguous calls when automated tools disagree or when the situation is genuinely unprecedented — a real but narrow residue relative to the course's full applied content. The rating holds High, hedged because entrepreneurship is inherently a domain of irreducible uncertainty where the value of direct human ownership of decisions may prove stickier than in more procedural business functions. No licensure or foundational constraint offers a firmer floor, and the capstone framing means the honest ten-year forecast rests heavily on how the entrepreneurship discipline itself evolves.
MGT 4430.d: Students learn the issues related to starting a business. It addresses three major topics: (1) all the tasks necessary to begin a startup venture, (2) growing a venture after the startup stage, and (3) managing a venture for survival, growth, or exit. This is the capstone course for the BA in Entrepreneurship degree.

r: This course examines how individuals and small groups behave in organizational settings and how organizations shape that behavior to pursue efficiency and effectiveness. The applied work is a mix of conceptual analysis of behavioral patterns, similar to the explanatory content task-exposure research treats as increasingly AI-deliverable, and the practical, interpersonal core of actually leading or motivating people, which remains a live, presence-dependent activity. Requiring MGT 3000 as a prerequisite, the course builds on general management concepts without itself feeding a further mandated sequence. There is no gen-ed designation and only a weak AACSB-level lock.
