At 24 months, AI can explain behavioral theories and generate case analyses competently, but the interpersonal application the course also trains is not something a model performs on the student's behalf. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI will fluently generate behavioral analysis, case-study interpretation, and diagnostic write-ups of organizational dynamics, eroding the course's explanatory and analytical content substantially. The interpersonal residue — actually motivating and coaching people, reading group dynamics in real time — is real but represents a modest fraction of a course whose graded work is largely written analysis and conceptual mastery, and the weak AACSB lock does not hold the rating down. Task-exposure research is instructive here: explanatory and writing-adjacent tasks sit near the exposed end of the spectrum, while the course's genuinely interpersonal leadership content is comparatively small. The rating rises to High, tracking the same pattern seen in MGT 3000, where the analytical bulk of managerial coursework automates well before its interpersonal core does.

A decade out, AI will be a capable interpreter of organizational-behavior theory and a fluent generator of behavioral case analysis, and the course's information-and-analysis rationale is substantially eroded in the central case. What remains is the durable, if narrower, human competence of actually leading and motivating people in real time — a residue this course also touches but does not center as its primary graded activity. The rating holds High, with the hedge that ten-year forecasts about how leadership skill is taught and assessed under ubiquitous AI carry real uncertainty. No licensure, foundational-scaffolding, or gen-ed constraint offers a floor here, so the trajectory tracks the exposed end of the business-course spectrum rather than the protected clinical or embodied end of the catalog.
MGT 4530.d: This course examines the behavior of individuals and small groups in organizational settings. The emphasis is on how organizations influence behavior in their quest for operating efficiency and effectiveness.

r: The course investigates matrix-organization concepts and project management, including the integrative decision making required across a product's life cycle. Scheduling, resource allocation, risk tracking, and status reporting — the operational backbone of project management — are exactly the kind of structured, data-driven tasks where controlled studies of AI-assisted coding and knowledge work show large speed gains, and dedicated project-management software already automates much of this. Coordinating people across a matrix structure, however, remains a live interpersonal-negotiation task. There is no licensure gate and only a weak AACSB-level lock. At 24 months the instrumental need to learn manual scheduling and tracking techniques is already softened by mature project-management software, though AI-specific integration into project workflows is still diffusing unevenly across firms. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI-assisted project-management platforms will competently generate schedules, flag risks, reallocate resources, and draft status reports from live project data, substantially automating the planning and tracking tasks this course centers on. The interpersonal work of coordinating people across a matrix organization's competing reporting lines persists as a real residue, but it is a narrower slice of the course's content than the scheduling and integrative-decision material, and the weak AACSB lock does not cap the rating. Observed-usage evidence on AI's concentration in computer-and-analytical work supports broad deployment into project-tracking tools specifically by this horizon. The rating rises to High: the applied planning tasks the course teaches are performed competently by AI with limited human input for routine projects, leaving negotiation and escalation as the residual human role.

A decade out, AI project-management agents will plausibly run much of the day-to-day scheduling, risk monitoring, and status communication for standard projects, with human project managers concentrated on stakeholder negotiation, escalation judgment, and genuinely novel project structures. The instrumental case for a course teaching manual project-management technique is substantially eroded under this trajectory. The rating holds High, hedged by uncertainty about how much organizations continue to value a human project manager as a single accountable point of contact even when the underlying planning work is automated — an organizational-trust consideration distinct from raw task capability. No foundational or institutional constraint offers a firmer floor for this course specifically, and the matrix-organization framing itself may shift meaningfully once AI participates directly in cross-functional coordination.
MGT 4550.d: This course investigates the concepts and applicability of matrix organizations and project management. The unique nature of the project-management structure is also examined, including its emphasis on integrative decision making throughout a product's life cycle.

r: This course covers identifying, measuring, and evaluating employee performance, using performance data for HR decisions, designing compensation systems, and aligning performance with organizational strategy. Compensation benchmarking, pay-structure modeling, and performance-metric analysis are quantitative, data-driven tasks that overlap directly with the Computer and Mathematical category observed-usage data identifies as AI's largest current-use area, and comp-analytics software already automates much of the benchmarking work. Delivering performance feedback and designing reward structures that motivate real people, however, keeps an interpersonal core in place. There is no gen-ed designation, and MGT 3530 gates entry without this course itself feeding further required coursework. At 24 months the analytical design work is already meaningfully AI-assisted, though firm-level adoption of AI specifically for compensation design remains uneven. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI will competently generate compensation benchmarks, pay-equity analyses, and performance-metric dashboards from organizational data, substantially automating the analytical design work this course teaches. The residue — communicating performance results to employees and defending compensation decisions in ambiguous cases — is real but represents a smaller share of the course's content than the design and evaluation methodology itself, and the weak AACSB lock does not cap the rating. Firm-level diffusion data suggests broader adoption of AI analytics tools across HR functions by this horizon, consistent with the course's applied tasks becoming largely automatable. The rating rises to High, paralleling the erosion seen in other quantitative-analytical business courses once near-term diffusion limits are no longer binding on this kind of analytical material.

A decade out, AI systems will plausibly design and continuously tune compensation structures and performance-measurement systems with limited human input for routine cases, leaving human HR professionals concentrated on contested pay decisions, legal-risk judgment calls, and communicating hard outcomes to employees. The instrumental case for a course centered on manual performance-metric design and compensation-system construction is substantially eroded under this trajectory. The rating holds High, hedged by genuine uncertainty about how much organizations continue to require human sign-off on compensation and performance decisions given their legal and morale stakes, which could sustain more hands-on training in this area than a pure capability read implies. No foundational or institutional lock offers a firmer floor here, unlike the sibling selection course down the hall.
MGT 4620.d: This course examines the management and reward of employee performance including methods of: (1) identifying, measuring and evaluating performance; (2) using performance data as a basis for human resource management decisions; and, (3) designing compensation systems to attract, retain, and motivate employees; and (4) ensuring strategic alignment of employee performance and organizational goals.

r: The course covers designing, implementing, and evaluating training and development programs, framed around the demands that global competition, multicultural and multinational workforces, and technology implementation place on developing employee and manager skill across all organizational levels. Instructional content creation — curriculum design, e-learning modules, training materials, skills-assessment instruments — is a writing-and-design task where productivity research already shows AI assistance producing substantial time savings and quality gains, and corporate learning platforms increasingly generate training content directly from a stated objective. Delivering and facilitating training in person, though, remains an interpersonal activity the course also addresses and grades. There is no gen-ed lock, and MGT 3530 is the only prerequisite. At 24 months the content-design work is meaningfully AI-assisted already, while live facilitation and organization-specific needs-assessment judgment remain comparatively resistant. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI will competently generate full training curricula, e-learning content, and skills-assessment materials tailored to a stated organizational context, substantially automating the design-and-development tasks this course centers on. The residue — facilitating live training sessions, coaching individuals through skill gaps, and diagnosing what a specific team actually needs beyond a generic template — persists but is a narrower slice of the graded course content than curriculum design itself, and the weak AACSB lock provides no cap on the rating. Productivity-research evidence on large AI-assisted writing gains extends naturally to instructional-content production of this kind. The rating rises to High: the applied design-and-development work the course teaches is performed competently by AI with limited human input for most standard, non-specialized training needs.

A decade out, AI will plausibly generate and continuously adapt training content and skills curricula with minimal human drafting, leaving human trainers and instructional designers concentrated on live facilitation, coaching, and organization-specific needs diagnosis that a generic model handles less well in practice. The instrumental case for a course centered on manually designing training programs is substantially eroded under this trajectory. The rating holds High, hedged by real uncertainty about how much organizations continue to value a human presence in delivering and coaching through training even once the underlying content is machine-generated — an interpersonal-trust factor distinct from raw content-production capability. No foundational-scaffolding or institutional lock offers a firmer floor for this specific course across the full decade of forecast uncertainty.
MGT 4640.d: This course focuses on the design, implementation, and uses of training and development as a necessary part of increasing the value of employee and manager skills. Rapid organizational change precipitated by global competition, multicultural and multinational workers, and technology implementation require organizations to develop the human potential and careers of their employees at all levels.

r: This course covers workforce planning, sourcing and recruiting talent, and the proper use of selection tools and procedures to hire effectively. Resume screening, candidate ranking, and structured-interview scoring are already meaningfully automated by applicant-tracking and algorithmic screening systems, placing much of the course's applied task set in the highly exposed category. But selection decisions carry serious legal exposure — adverse-impact and discrimination liability under employment law — where a confidently wrong algorithmic recommendation is a non-obvious failure with real consequences, precisely the verification-burden condition the jagged-frontier evidence warns about. That elevated verification requirement drops this course a full band relative to its sibling HR courses at this horizon. There is no gen-ed lock. At 24 months the instrumental need for a human who understands proper selection procedure and its legal boundaries is intact. Rating Low.

By 2031, algorithmic and AI-driven candidate screening will be more capable and more widely deployed, and observed-usage data continues to show hiring-adjacent evaluative tasks well within the analytical categories AI increasingly handles. Yet the same legal-liability structure persists: a biased or poorly validated selection tool creates disparate-impact exposure that only a human trained in proper selection methodology and its legal boundaries can catch, and that verification burden does not relax on a five-year clock even as underlying screening technology improves. The weak AACSB lock does not itself hold the rating down; the elevated verification requirement does that work instead. The rating rises to Medium, reflecting substantial automation of the mechanical screening tasks alongside the persistence of a real oversight function.

A decade out, AI-driven selection tools will plausibly handle most routine candidate screening, ranking, and initial assessment, and the instrumental rationale for teaching students to perform these tasks manually is substantially eroded. The verification residue — validating that a selection process is legally defensible and free of disparate impact — becomes proportionally more of what the course's remaining value is about, but this is a narrower, oversight-oriented competence rather than the full breadth of the current course. The rating reaches High only at this horizon, one step later than its sibling HR courses, reflecting how the legal-liability verification burden holds erosion back longer here than for compensation or training design. Confidence is moderate given genuine uncertainty about how employment-discrimination law and algorithmic-hiring regulation co-evolve over a full decade.
MGT 4660.d: This course introduces students to issues related to the selection and placement of employees, including workforce planning issues, sourcing and recruiting talent, and the proper use of selection tools and procedures that will facilitate the effective selection of talent.

r: This course examines the political, economic, sociocultural, technological, and legal dimensions of the global business environment, how cultures vary, and how cross-national institutional differences shape global strategy. The work is predominantly analytical and expository — synthesizing country-level context, comparing institutional environments, evaluating global-strategy options — content squarely inside the categories task-exposure research finds most exposed, since it resembles the writing and synthesis work AI already performs competently. It requires MGT 3820 and several coreqs, but it is a study-and-analysis course, not embodied cross-cultural fieldwork, so little protects it beyond near-term diffusion limits and the weak AACSB lock. At 24 months, AI already drafts competent country and institutional analysis, but firms and programs have not yet restructured around it. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI will fluently synthesize country-risk analysis, cross-cultural comparisons, and global-strategy options from available data, substantially automating the analytical and expository work this course centers on. Task-exposure research consistently finds this kind of comparative, writing-heavy analysis among the most exposed activities, and no embodiment, licensure, or foundational-scaffolding constraint holds the rating down — the weak AACSB lock provides no cap, and the several coreqs required alongside this course do not amount to an institutional mandate. The residue is judgment in genuinely novel or high-stakes cross-border situations where cultural nuance and negotiation matter, a real but narrower competence than producing the comparative analysis itself. The rating rises to High, consistent with the pattern seen in other analytical, non-foundational business and social-science courses once near-term diffusion limits are no longer binding.

A decade out, AI will generate sophisticated comparative institutional and cross-cultural strategic analysis on demand, and the applied synthesis work to which this course's knowledge is put is substantially performed by AI in the central case. With no protective constraint binding — no embodiment, no licensure, no foundational role — the instrumental case for the course as currently structured is substantially eroded. The rating is High, hedged by genuine ten-year uncertainty and by the possibility that direct human relationship-building and negotiation across cultures retains a premium that pure country-analysis automation does not replace in practice. The intrinsic value of cross-cultural competence for its own sake is real but distinct from the instrumental task-substitution question this particular rating is explicitly scoped to address here.
MGT 4700.d: In this course, students learn about the broad variety of opportunities and challenges that managers face as they explore the global business environment - in particular, the political, economic, sociocultural, technological and legal aspects. They investigate the ways in which cultures vary and how to manage effectively in these diverse environments. Students examine topics such as the challenges of creating global strategies and the implications of cross-national differences in institutional environments.

r: This course develops students' capacity to contextualize and challenge workforce systems that perpetuate racial, gender, and intersectional inequity, using active listening and dialogue as its core method, with students leading each other to interrogate power, privilege, and discrimination in the workplace. The applied work is live, dialogic, and relational — real-time interpersonal engagement with sensitive, values-laden material — precisely the embodied, presence-dependent activity task-exposure research treats as least automatable, even though supporting readings and case analysis are more exposed. There is no gen-ed designation, and the course is a terminal senior-level elective. At 24 months the instrumental need for the human dialogic process the course is built around is essentially untouched by AI capability growth; the pedagogy itself resists substitution. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI could plausibly generate competent case studies, background research, and even discussion prompts about workplace inequity, but the course's actual applied activity — students practicing active listening, leading each other through dialogue, and developing the interpersonal skill to promote change in real workplaces — remains a live, embodied competence no model performs on a learner's behalf. Verification matters here too: a confidently generated but tone-deaf or oversimplified AI treatment of discrimination and privilege carries real reputational and relational risk, the kind of non-obvious failure the jagged-frontier evidence warns about, keeping trained human facilitation necessary. Neither the weak AACSB lock nor any foundational role does the protective work; the dialogic method itself does. The rating stays Low across this horizon.

A decade out, AI will be a fluent generator of written analysis on workplace inequity and discrimination, but the specific competence this course cultivates — a person's own capacity for active listening, dialogic engagement, and skillful navigation of sensitive interpersonal territory around power and privilege — is not a task AI performs for the student; it is inherently embodied, real-time, and relational. The genuine uncertainty is in how supporting materials and case content are sourced under ubiquitous AI, not in whether the dialogic skill-building core requires direct human practice, which the evidence continues to support. The rating holds Low with the honest caveat that no institutional mandate protects this course; its durability rests entirely on the embodied, presence-dependent nature of the pedagogy itself, not on any accreditation or gen-ed lock.
MGT 4830.d: Students contextualize, understand and challenge workforce systems and management practices that perpetuate racial, gender and intersectional inequity and stand in the way of achieving social justice. In this dynamic course, students use the skills of active listening and dialogue to develop their understanding of the history of social justice in the U.S. Students lead each other to interrogate and challenge how positions of power and privilege created by a colonizing culture continue to oppress marginalized groups in the workforce. Students collectively and critically analyze how oppressive systems result in higher barriers to entry, differential performance reviews, hostile work environments and illegal discrimination for members of marginalized groups in the workplace. Students learn from the efforts and successes of past and present social justice advocates and solidarity movements, and they develop the skills to promote social justice in today's workplace.

r: MGT 4850 asks students to run an actual consulting engagement: build rapport with a client, scan the organizational environment for trends, diagnose problems, and draft recommended alternatives. The analytical and drafting portions, trend scanning, structuring alternatives, writing recommendation memos, overlap with tasks task-exposure research classifies as positively associated with exposure, since programming and writing skills correlate most strongly with automatability, and generative tools already produce competent first-draft business analysis. But the course's defining activity is establishing rapport with a real client and reading their specific organizational context in person, a real-time interpersonal task current systems do not perform; GDPval shows even top models still fall short of expert parity on full real-world deliverables. With no general-studies designation and only AACSB's non-course-specific accreditation attaching, institutional lock-in is weak, but the embodied client relationship remains the course's core deliverable at this horizon.

By 2031, drafting tools for environmental scanning, SWOT-style trend identification, and recommendation memos will likely be routine inputs to a consulting engagement, and observed-usage data already shows office and analytical writing tasks concentrated in AI use, suggesting further diffusion despite Census BTOS finding only a minority of firms formally using AI as of late 2025. Students will increasingly treat AI as a drafting collaborator for the diagnostic and alternatives-generation steps MGT 4850 teaches. Yet the course's grading center of gravity, building rapport with an actual client, reading unstated organizational politics, and adapting recommendations in real time during service-learning interactions, stays embodied and interpersonal, a task category task-exposure research and the jagged-frontier literature both treat as resistant, since AI users perform worse outside the model's competence frontier and misjudge when that boundary has been crossed. The instrumental case for the course softens but does not collapse.

Ten years out, capability trends documented by METR and Epoch, task-time horizons roughly doubling every four to seven months, point toward AI handling longer, more autonomous analytical workflows, so the diagnostic and report-writing scaffolding of a consulting engagement could be substantially pre-drafted before a student ever meets a client. That would compress, but not eliminate, MGT 4850's instrumental value, because the course is built around an embodied, real-time interpersonal skill, earning a client's trust and adapting live to their specific small-business context, that has shown no comparable trajectory of AI substitution in the available evidence and remains outside what GDPval-style deliverable evaluations currently test. Absent a general-studies or accreditation lock, AACSB alone imposes no course-specific mandate, the course's durability rests entirely on this interpersonal core rather than institutional protection. Confidence in this projection is necessarily limited given how much norms around AI-mediated client interaction could shift.
MGT 4850.d: This course introduces students to the consulting process and requires them to apply its steps to an actual organization or small business. Students develop skills in building rapport with clients, identifying major trends in a client's organizational environment, identifying the major problems or issues facing a client organization, developing viable alternatives, and formulating and recommending solutions to the problems or issues identified. There is a service learning component where students apply course concepts to an actual business setting and reflect on their service experiences.

r: MGT 4910 teaches frameworks for visualizing individual, group, organizational, and societal systems and for building a transformational vision, then asks students to plan how they would communicate that vision to mobilize people. The framework-building and vision-articulation work, diagnosing a system, drafting a vision statement, structuring a change narrative, is substantially writing- and analysis-based, the category task-exposure research finds most positively associated with exposure, and productivity studies already show professional writing tasks completed faster with AI assistance while quality holds or improves. Generative tools can already produce competent multi-level organizational diagnoses and vision drafts from case inputs. What AI cannot yet do is the course's ultimate target skill: actually garnering people's energy through live communication and judgment under ambiguity. At this horizon the instrumental need for the course is already meaningfully reduced for the conceptual half of the material, with no general-studies or accreditation mandate to offset it.

By 2031, AI systems will likely draft polished leadership-framework analyses and vision statements routinely, consistent with observed-usage data showing writing and structured-analysis tasks concentrated among the most AI-touched activities, and with roughly half of jobs already having a meaningful share of tasks touched by current models. Strategic Leadership's content, frameworks for visualizing human systems, transformation narratives, sits squarely in that exposed territory, so the course's lecture-and-case material could be substituted for a student capable of prompting for equivalent analysis. The course carries no general-studies designation and only AACSB's weak, non-course-specific accreditation lock, so no institutional backstop protects it. What continues to justify taking it is the practiced judgment behind mobilizing real people, which jagged-frontier findings suggest AI still handles unevenly and which the evidence base does not show migrating to automated systems at comparable pace. The rating reflects that gap narrowing, not closing.

A ten-year horizon is long relative to observed capability growth, METR and Epoch data show AI task-time horizons roughly doubling every four to seven months, so it is plausible that leadership-framework instruction, vision drafting, and even simulated stakeholder-communication exercises are substantially AI-mediated by 2036. Because MGT 4910 has no general-studies designation and AACSB accreditation does not mandate this specific course, no institutional lock-in tempers that trajectory the way it would for a licensure-gated course. The scenario is not confidently predictable, however: task-exposure research consistently finds critical-thinking- and judgment-heavy work negatively associated with exposure even as writing-heavy work rises, and leading through ambiguity sits closer to the former than the latter in practice, even where the conceptual scaffolding taught here sits closer to the latter. Any projection this far out should be read as a probable direction under continued diffusion, not a settled outcome, given adoption has so far lagged raw capability.
MGT 4910.d: Leaders are expected to be visionary. This course provides participants with frameworks to visualize human systems and processes at multiple levels such as individual, relationship, group, organization and society. Such visualization is a prerequisite to discovery of leadership opportunities for the participants and to developing a vision of transformation of these human systems. A leader's job is to communicate the vision to garner people's energy and to facilitate the processes of transformation.

r: MGT 4950 is the College of Business capstone, styled a Senior Experience, requiring students to integrate accounting, finance, information systems, economics, management, and marketing knowledge into strategic recommendations for domestic and global organizations, with some sections adding a service-learning client engagement. The component analytical tasks, competitive analysis, scenario development, drafting a strategic plan, fall into the writing- and analysis-heavy category task-exposure research associates most strongly with exposure, and generative tools already produce credible first-draft strategic analyses from case data. But the course's actual assessed task is cross-functional synthesis under real client constraints, including, in service-learning sections, in-person client interaction and defense of recommendations, an embodied and high-stakes activity where GDPval-style evaluations still show top models below expert parity on complete deliverables. With no general-studies designation and only AACSB's non-course-specific accreditation attaching, the course's durability currently rests on that integrative, client-facing core rather than institutional protection.

By 2031, AI assistance for the individual analytical inputs to a strategic plan, market and competitive analysis, financial projections, drafting the plan document, will likely be routine, consistent with observed-usage data showing office and analytical writing concentrated among AI's most common uses and with adoption continuing to diffuse from the roughly one-fifth of firms already using it in some form. That erodes some of the instrumental case for MGT 4950's component tasks. What remains distinctly human is the capstone's integrative judgment across business disciplines applied to a specific, ambiguous organization, plus, in service-learning sections, live client interaction, tasks where jagged-frontier evidence suggests AI users perform meaningfully worse once outside a narrow competence frontier and often fail to recognize it. Because no general-studies or licensure lock offsets a still-weak AACSB requirement, the course's protection is functional rather than institutional, and that function is narrowing but not gone.

Ten years is enough time, given METR- and Epoch-documented growth in AI task-time horizons, for substantially more of a capstone strategic-planning workflow to be AI-assisted end to end, including longer autonomous analysis chains across the accounting, finance, and marketing inputs the course integrates. Because the course carries no general-studies designation and AACSB accreditation imposes no course-specific mandate, institutional lock-in would not meaningfully slow that substitution if it occurs. Still, the course's defining task is contextualized synthesis and, in service-learning sections, live client engagement and defense of recommendations under real stakes, activities the available evidence does not show migrating to automation at the pace of drafting or analysis subtasks, and macro-level productivity effects from AI diffusion remain modest per current estimates. This is a genuinely uncertain projection at a ten-year remove; it should be read as directional, reflecting continued but uneven erosion of the course's instrumental necessity.
MGT 4950.d: Students are introduced to concepts used by managers to develop companies that can prosper in a competitive, global environment. Students are provided the opportunity to apply the concepts and theories of strategic management along with knowledge gained from business courses, general studies, and work experience to the operating and strategic changes faced by domestic and global organizations (Senior Experience). Some sections include a service learning (SL) component where students apply course concepts involving an actual business client and are required to reflect on their service learning experience.
